figures.caption: FIG. 3. Equal-time CDW correlation function C(R, t) versus scaled separation R = x/L(t) at t = 40, 80, 160, and 320, obtained from KPM reference dynamics (left) and GRNN predictions (right). The GRNN captures the spatial correlation profiles, while the collapse of curves at different times in both panels demonstrates dynamical scaling.

FIG. 4. Autoregressive GRNN simulation of CDW domain coarsening on a 200 × 200 lattice at t = 0, 80, and 6400. Color indicates the local order parameter ϕ on the scale shown at right, from −1 to 1. The initially disordered field evolves into domains of the two symmetry-related charge-ordered states.

FIG. 5. One-step GRNN computation. Graph layers aggregate neighboring physical features into the embedding zi(t); the graph-coupled GRU combines this embedding with local and neighboring hidden states to produce h+ i ≡ hi(t+1). The readout MLP uses zi(t) and the updated memory to predict δi(t), which enters the physical update map Rϕ. The upper bypass carries the present physical field directly to this map. Spatial and recurrent aggregation are indicated by orange and violet paths, respectively. All learned parameters are shared across lattice sites.

FIG. 6. Microscopic lattice pattern and emergent Ising-like CDW field in a representative 40×40 configuration. Left: displacement Qi, whose alternating pattern tracks the local charge modulation through electron–lattice coupling. Right: staggered neighbor-density contrast ϕi = (−1)xi+yi(ni− 1 4 ∑ j∈Ni nj) evaluated for the same configuration. The staggered factor removes the checkerboard oscillation, so red and blue regions mark the two symmetry-related CDW domains; intermediate values occur near domain walls. The color bars show the values plotted in each panel.
TABLE I. Model and reference-trajectory settings. The damping value refers to the integrator setting; no numerical value for γ in Eq. (B1) is inferred from it.

FIG. 7. Time-dependent structure factor S(q, t) of the staggered CDW field on a 40× 40 lattice. The upper row shows KPM reference trajectories and the lower row shows autoregressive GRNN predictions at t = 0, 40, and 400 (left to right). Momentum is measured relative to the checkerboard ordering wave vector, so the ordering peak of the staggered field is centered at q = 0. Its narrowing as time increases reflects growing CDW domains; the GRNN reproduces the corresponding momentum-space pattern. Dashed squares outline the first Brillouin zone.
TABLE II. GRNN architecture and training settings used for the Holstein demonstration.

FIG. 8. Ablation study of the graph-recurrent neural network architecture. Temporal autocorrelation functions A(τ) predicted by five candidate models (C1–C5) are compared with the KPM reference. The candidates differ in their use of recurrent memory and spatially aggregated hidden states, as summarized in Table III. The full GRNN architecture (C5) and the model with spatially coupled recurrent gates (C3) exhibit the closest agreement with the reference dynamics.

TABLE III. Comparison of the candidate architectures considered in the ablation study. All models use the same GNN backbone with feature dimensions 1 → 128 → 96 → 64. Recurrent models employ a hidden-state dimension of 96. The RMSE quantifies the discrepancy between the predicted temporal autocorrelation function and the KPM reference.
